title: Enabling Ahead Prediction with Practical Energy Constraints
problem: Branch predictors require multiple pipeline cycles to produce a prediction, causing a latency penalty; ahead prediction solves this by starting early but must consider all 2^N possible histories for the N intermediate branches, increasing energy by 14.6x and making the approach impractical.
motivation: Branch misprediction penalties dominate front-end stalls in modern out-of-order processors, and latency-reducing ahead prediction has been dismissed due to prohibitive energy cost.
method: The authors observe that most of the 2^N possible intermediate branch-direction combinations never actually occur at runtime; only one or two patterns are observed in practice. They modify the TAGE predictor to track and eliminate non-materializing history patterns, reducing the number of parallel prediction paths that must be evaluated. This allows the ahead predictor to operate with only 1.5x energy overhead instead of the previously assumed 14.6x, while delivering 4.4% IPC improvement.
key_novelty: Observation that intermediate branch history patterns rarely materialize reduces the effective branching factor of ahead prediction from exponential to near-constant, making practical ahead prediction feasible.
contributions: Characterization showing that intermediate branch directions rarely produce more than one or two distinct observed history patterns
Modified TAGE predictor that filters non-materializing intermediate history combinations
Practical ahead predictor achieving 4.4% performance improvement at only 1.5x energy overhead (vs. 14.6x naive)
Demonstration that ahead prediction is energy-viable for deployment in real processor pipelines
limitations: Not discussed explicitly; generalization across diverse workload types beyond the evaluated benchmarks is not assessed.
